content.thinking:
I need to be careful not to cite specific figures myself, instead referencing the placeholder series values. The impact is clear: latency rose while errors stayed unchanged, with account pages slowing down over the incident duration — I should describe the p95 trend using the series placeholders rather than actual numbers or units, and avoid phrasing like "10x" in favor of referencing the computed multiplier placeholder.

For causation, the diff showing the quadratic recompute loop is a verified fact (not an unverified reading), and the rollback's confirmed recovery timestamps support the chain, so I'd call it true but note the quadratic-cost mechanism itself comes from reading code rather than profiling. I'm also ruling out the earlier unrelated change, since it preceded the onset by hours, the flag provider showing no recent changes, and baseline error levels indicating no failure spike.

For contributing factors, I'm flagging the missing pre-deploy performance test (only correctness was checked), the alert delay from the rule's wait period, and auto-sync being disabled so nothing merged reaches the affected system — each needs a corresponding action item: a new test bounding time/reads for long purchase histories, the existing fix action, the auto-sync fix, and possibly a canary latency comparison for better detection since error-rate monitoring wouldn't have caught this. I'm also noting the time from onset to alert includes the rule's wait period, and reminding myself to avoid writing out number words like "one" where possible.

I should steer clear of spelling out percentile figures like "p95" and instead say "tail latency," use the full revision hash rather than truncating it, and swap specific timestamps for placeholders.

action_items.item: Add a performance test for account-page spend functions that runs a very long purchase history and fails if the number of price reads or the run time grows faster than linearly with the number of purchases.
Add a post-deploy check that compares account-page tail latency on the new revision with the previous one, and rolls back or alerts on a rise even when the error rate is flat.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw slow account pages from {began} to {back_to_normal}. The tail-latency series behind the HighLatency alert went from {series_before} to an average of {series_while_broken} and a worst of {series_at_worst}. Failed requests did not rise: the error rate was {errors_while_broken} while broken against {errors_before} before, and the error log lines were at their usual baseline, so this was slowness rather than failure.
The slowdown began in the same minute that revision 5e07d73148d0a704b8fefe5f379bc652bb773655 was deployed to io-shop.

That revision changed average_spend_per_item. It now recomputes the running total inside a loop, summing purchases[:index+1] for every purchase, and only the last pass's value is used. Before it, the function made a single division using the account's carried total.

Because each pass re-reads all earlier purchases, the work grows quadratically with purchase history, so shoppers with long histories paid most of the cost on the account page. This is a static reading of the code. No profile or run in the record confirms the exact cost.

The release is the trigger and not something else. The earlier deploy was hours before the onset, and the flag provider showed no recent flag changes. Errors stayed at baseline, which does not point to failures. Rolling back the revision was judged confirmed because the service was no longer at the incident's level from {back_to_normal}.

contributing_factors.factor: The tests added with the change checked only that the figure was correct (including a drifted-total case). No test or check on cost with a long purchase history was seen in the record, so the quadratic loop passed.

No comparison of latency before and after rollout was seen. The slowdown was found only through the paging rule, which waits {rule_waits} before firing, and the alert was raised at {alert_raised}. Error rate did not move, so an error-based signal would not have shown it.
Automatic sync of io-shop is off, so nothing merged reaches it until it is turned back on. A merged fix would not be deployed, and the rollback stays in place.

input.executive_summary: For a short period after a new version of the shop was released, account pages loaded much more slowly than usual. The slowdown lasted {duration}. The people affected were shoppers who opened account pages. The record shows no extra failed requests, so pages still loaded, only slowly. The tail-latency series that paged us averaged {series_while_broken} while the fault lasted and peaked at {series_at_worst}, against {series_before} before. Argus rolled the release back, and the metrics showed the service back to normal at {back_to_normal}. A draft fix was proposed for review.

got_lucky: No more requests failed than before, so the harm was slowness only. The response did not depend on an error-rate alert, which would not have fired.
went_well: Argus tied the onset to the deploy within seconds, using the change history and the diff.
The rollback was confirmed from the metrics, and the service was back to normal at {back_to_normal}.
A draft fix pull request was proposed soon after mitigation.
went_wrong: A change made only for correctness added a quadratic cost, and no check on cost was seen before it reached production.
The alert came only after the paging rule's wait, so shoppers were slowed for part of the time before anyone was paged.

input.root_cause: The deploy of revision 5e07d73148d0a704b8fefe5f379bc652bb773655 rewrote average_spend_per_item to re-sum the purchase list inside a loop (purchases[:index+1] on every pass) and keep only the last pass. Work therefore grows quadratically with purchase history, so account pages for shoppers with long histories rendered slowly. This reading comes from the diff; the cost was not profiled. The tests added with the change checked only that the figure was correct, so nothing in the record caught the extra cost before release.
input.symptom: Account pages were slow to load
